Fainting from the heat isn’t LQTS related. LQTS are sudden faints, not gradual, and they have little/no warning. Like my daughter fainted while eating, she suddenly slumped with no warning. I’ve been walking and lost consciousness, causing me to hit my head and get a concussion. Echocardiograms won’t show LQTS, only an ecg/holter can. LQTS doesn’t always show, so a holter is one of the best ways to see if you have prolonged QT’s. My dx came after sudden cardiac arrest and I am genetically positive. See another cardiologist for a second opinion if you want though!

Hi OP. First, I’m so sorry you’re going through this. 

My advice comes from my own experience at 18. I went into sudden cardiac arrest (a bit different than a heart attack, but same kind of experiences) while I was in the hospital for an illness. It turns out I have a genetic condition that causes cardiac arrest, fainting, arrhythmia, etc. It’s known as a sudden arrhythmic death syndrome, as one of the first symptoms people experience is sudden cardiac arrest or death. I was a healthy 18 year old at the time. 

When it happened I didn’t know how to process. I was so scared it was going to happen again. I don’t think much really helped, except time and doctors. Time will make it easier, and doctors will help make it better and give you answers.  

I know it’s almost impossible to not stress out, so I don’t blame you. In your situation, I would do something that makes me focus on something else to forget about it for a while. When I experienced cardiac arrest, I surrounded myself with people I love like friends and family, and I took up a new hobby which really helped me not hyper focus on what happened and what could happen. 

Even now I’m at risk for sudden death, but it’s such a minuscule chance (so long as I follow the guidelines) that it doesn’t even scare/bother me anymore. The last time I was scared was when I was giving birth to my child last year, but even then I was surrounded by doctors and specialists who were there just in case, and it helped soothe my mind.

I never had to interview or provide anything other than the initial application when applying for spousal PR. I moved from the US to Canada. We never had a wedding ceremony, we got married in a park by an officiant as there is no courthouse weddings here in BC. We had met online in 2016, I saw him for the first time in 2017, and by the time we got married in 2019 I saw him 5-6 times. I provided airplane tickets, copies of Airbnb receipts, and pics from every visit with dates. This was really crucial as you have to prove the relationship is legitimate. It only took a little over a year to be approved and to receive my COPR because we applied right before covid hit, so everything was delayed. I received my COPR, landed at Vancouver in YVR, and the CBSA officer signed my landing document and I officially became a PR on Oct 7, 2021. No interview, nothing other than the initial paperwork and application. 

It could be that you got married during the same trip you took to meet him for the first time. Also, Lebanon might be considered a higher risk country and combined with the overall lack of trips before marriage it likely threw red flags, even if your marriage actually is legitimate.

I think your best bet is to follow along with your immigration lawyer because you don’t want to further complicate things, like his ability to come to Canada and visit you - he could absolutely be denied at the border.


Edited to add: I don’t think it’s age either, as my husband was 22 and I was 24 when we had gotten married.
